title: Cincinnatus Returns to His Plow
text:
In 458 BC, according to the Roman historian Livy, a Roman army under the consul Minucius was trapped by the Aequi in a mountain valley. The Senate decided the city needed a dictator, a temporary ruler with near-absolute power, and chose Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus, a former consul who was then working a small farm of about four acres across the Tiber.

Livy says the envoys found him at work in the field, digging or plowing. He asked his wife Racilia to bring his toga from the cottage, wiped off the dust and sweat, and put it on to hear the Senate's message. He was saluted as dictator and taken into the city.

He acted quickly. He ordered every man of military age to assemble before sunset with food and stakes, marched through the night, and surrounded the enemy who were surrounding the Romans. The Aequi surrendered and were made to pass under a yoke of spears.

The dictatorship could legally last six months. Livy reports that Cincinnatus resigned it after sixteen days and went back to his farm.
lesson: Authority given for a task should be returned when the task is done. Holding power only as long as it is needed earns more trust than any title.
location: Rome and the Alban Hills (modern Italy)
source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita, Book 3, chapters 26 to 29
caveat: Early Roman history in Livy mixes tradition and legend, and the details of this episode cannot be verified.
